copy.name: How to calculate standard deviation
copy.blurb: Sample or population, step by step.
copy.title: How to calculate standard deviation
copy.lead: The standard deviation tells you how far values typically sit from their mean. You will find the mean, measure each value's distance from it, average the squared distances and take the square root, and learn when to divide by n − 1 instead of n.
copy.result: The standard deviation, variance and standard error of any list of numbers, worked out by hand and checked with the calculator.
copy.note: The standard deviation is pulled up by outliers. With strongly skewed data, report the median and the range alongside it.
copy.s1t: Open the Standard deviation calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Paste your numbers, one list, separated by spaces, commas or new lines. The example is 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.
copy.s2b: Add the values and divide by how many there are: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
copy.s3t: Square each distance from the mean
copy.s3b: Subtract the mean from every value and square the result: 2 − 5 = −3 gives 9, 4 − 5 = −1 gives 1, and so on. Squaring stops the negatives from cancelling the positives. The squares add up to 32.
copy.s4b: For a sample from a larger group divide by n − 1: 32 ÷ 7 = 4.571 is the sample variance. Only when you have every member of the group divide by n: 32 ÷ 8 = 4 is the population variance.
copy.s5b: The square root of the variance is the standard deviation: √4.571 = 2.138 for the sample, √4 = 2 for the population. It is in the same units as your data.
copy.s6b: Report the mean with it: M = 5.00, SD = 2.14. The standard error of the mean is SD ÷ √n = 0.76; it is what confidence intervals use. The calculator's table shows every step.
copy.diagram1: Each value's distance from the mean of 5; the squared distances add up to 32.
copy.diagram2: Divide the sum of squares by n − 1 for a sample or n for a population, then take the square root.

faq.q1: What is the formula for standard deviation?
faq.a1: s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)) for a sample and σ = √(Σ(x − μ)² ÷ n) for a population: the square root of the average squared distance from the mean.
faq.q2: Why divide by n − 1 for a sample?
faq.a2: A sample's own mean sits closer to its values than the true population mean does, so dividing by n would underestimate the spread. Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) makes up for it.
faq.q3: What is a good standard deviation?
faq.a3: There is no good or bad value on its own. Compare it with the mean (the coefficient of variation) or with other groups measured on the same scale.
faq.q4: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
faq.a4: The standard deviation describes the spread of individual values. The standard error (SD ÷ √n) describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.
faq.q5: How do I find standard deviation in Excel or Google Sheets?
faq.a5: Use STDEV.S for a sample and STDEV.P for a population (STDEV and STDEVP in older versions).

copy.name: How to calculate sample size
copy.title: How to calculate sample size for a survey
copy.lead: A sample that is too small gives wide, unreliable results; one that is too big wastes time. You will set a confidence level and margin of error, use Cochran's formula, adjust for a small population, see what Slovin's formula does, and plan for people who do not answer.
copy.result: The number of completed responses your study needs and how many people to invite.
copy.note: These formulas assume a simple random sample. Quota, convenience or cluster samples need other methods; ask your supervisor or a statistician.
copy.s1t: Open the Sample size calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Choose the method: a proportion (Cochran) for yes/no and percentage questions, Slovin's formula, or a mean when you know the standard deviation.
copy.s2t: Choose the confidence level and margin of error
copy.s2b: 95 % confidence (z = 1.96) and a ±5 % margin are the usual choices. A smaller margin needs a much larger sample: halving it roughly quadruples n.
copy.s3b: n₀ = z² × p(1 − p) ÷ e². With no earlier estimate, use p = 50 %, which gives the largest sample: 1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05² = 384.2, rounded up to 385.
copy.s4b: When you know the population size N, use n = n₀ ÷ (1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N). For N = 1,000, n₀ = 384.2 becomes 278. For very large populations the correction changes almost nothing.
copy.s5b: Slovin's n = N ÷ (1 + N × e²) gives 286 for N = 1,000 and e = 5 %. It fixes p at 50 % and ignores the confidence level, so many reviewers prefer Cochran's formula; use Slovin when your department asks for it.
copy.s6b: Divide the sample size by the share of people you expect to answer: 385 at a 40 % response rate means inviting 963. Report the formula, its inputs and the final number in your methods section.
copy.diagram1: The sample needed at 95 % confidence grows fast as the margin of error shrinks.
copy.diagram2: Cochran's formula at 95 % confidence, a ±5 % margin and p = 50 %.

faq.q1: What sample size do I need for a survey?
faq.a1: For a large population, 95 % confidence and a ±5 % margin, about 385 completed responses. Smaller populations need fewer; enter yours in the calculator.
faq.a2: n = N ÷ (1 + N × e²), with N the population size and e the margin of error. It is common in theses in Indonesia and the Philippines but ignores the confidence level and the expected proportion.
faq.a3: p(1 − p) is largest at 50 %, so it gives the safest sample when you do not know the answer in advance.
faq.q4: Does a bigger population need a bigger sample?
faq.a4: Only up to a point. Above roughly 20,000 people the required sample barely changes: 385 is enough for a city and for a country at the same precision.
faq.q5: How do I calculate sample size for comparing two groups?
faq.a5: That needs a power analysis with the effect size you expect, α and the power you want (often 80 %). It is a different calculation from these survey formulas.

copy.name: How to calculate Cronbach's alpha
copy.title: How to calculate Cronbach's alpha
copy.lead: Cronbach's alpha shows whether the items of a questionnaire scale measure the same thing. You will arrange the scores, see how alpha is calculated, read it against common thresholds, find weak items and report the result.
copy.result: Alpha for your scale, a judgement of its internal consistency, and a list of items worth a second look.
copy.note: Alpha assumes the items measure one idea and are scored in the same direction. A high alpha does not prove the scale measures what you intend; that is validity.
copy.s1t: Open the Cronbach's alpha calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Copy the item columns from Excel, Google Sheets or SPSS and paste them: one row per respondent, one column per item, with or without a header row.
copy.s2b: If agreeing with an item means the opposite of the others, flip its scores before pasting. On a 1–5 scale the new score is 6 minus the old one.
copy.s3b: α = k ÷ (k − 1) × (1 − Σ item variances ÷ variance of the total score), where k is the number of items. When items move together, the total varies much more than the items do separately, and alpha rises.
copy.s4b: The example scale (5 items, 10 respondents) has α = 0.935. A common rule of thumb: 0.9 and above excellent, 0.8 good, 0.7 acceptable, 0.6 questionable, 0.5 poor. Many fields want at least 0.7.
copy.s5b: Look at the corrected item-total correlation (below about 0.3 is weak) and alpha if item deleted. An item whose removal raises alpha (marked ↑) may not fit the scale, or may still need recoding.
copy.s6b: Write the number of items and respondents with it: "The scale showed excellent internal consistency, Cronbach's α = .93 (5 items, n = 10)." Report alpha for each subscale separately.
copy.diagram1: Item scores in rows and columns: alpha compares the item variances with the variance of the total.
copy.diagram2: Common thresholds for Cronbach's alpha, with the example scale at 0.935.

faq.q1: What is a good Cronbach's alpha?
faq.a1: 0.7 or higher is usually acceptable, 0.8 good and 0.9 excellent. Values above about 0.95 can mean the items repeat each other.
faq.a2: Yes, usually because some items are reverse-worded and not recoded, or because the items do not measure the same thing.
faq.q3: How many items does Cronbach's alpha need?
faq.a3: At least two, but alpha is more stable with three or more. It also rises with the number of items, so a long scale can look reliable even when its items correlate weakly.
faq.a4: Alpha computed from the average correlation between items instead of their variances. It is useful when items use different scales.
faq.q5: How do I calculate Cronbach's alpha in SPSS?
faq.a5: Analyze → Scale → Reliability Analysis, move the items in, choose Alpha, and tick "Scale if item deleted" under Statistics.

copy.name: How to do a t-test
copy.title: How to do a t-test
copy.lead: A t-test asks whether a difference in means is larger than chance would explain. You will choose the right t-test, enter the data, read t, the degrees of freedom and the p-value, add an effect size and report the result.
copy.result: A t-test for your data with its p-value, confidence interval, Cohen's d and an APA-style sentence.
copy.note: t-tests assume roughly normal data within each group, or groups large enough (about 30 or more) for that not to matter much. With small, skewed samples consider a non-parametric test.
copy.s1t: Open the T-test calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Choose the test: one-sample compares one group with a fixed value, independent samples compares two separate groups, and paired compares two measurements of the same people.
copy.s2b: Paste each group's numbers. For a paired test list both measurements in the same order, so each before value sits opposite its after value.
copy.s3b: Welch's test does not assume equal variances and is the safer default, which is why the calculator starts with it. Student's pooled test assumes equal variances and gives whole-number degrees of freedom.
copy.s4b: The example groups give t(13.71) = 1.87, p = .082. The p-value is the chance of a difference at least this large if there were no real difference; .082 is above .05, so the difference is not statistically significant.
copy.s5t: Add the interval and the effect size
copy.s5b: The 95 % confidence interval for the difference, −0.06 to 0.91, includes 0, which matches the non-significant result. Cohen's d = 0.94 is a large difference, so a bigger sample might well find it significant.
copy.s6b: Give the means and SDs, then t, df, p and d: "Group A (M = 5.61, SD = 0.49) did not differ significantly from group B (M = 5.19, SD = 0.42), t(13.71) = 1.87, p = .082, d = 0.94." Copy the APA line from the calculator.
copy.diagram1: Which t-test to use: one group against a value, two separate groups, or the same people twice.
copy.diagram2: The t distribution: the shaded tails beyond ±1.87 make up the two-tailed p-value of .082.

faq.a1: One-sample for one group against a known value, independent samples for two separate groups, and paired for two measurements of the same people or matched pairs.
faq.q2: What does the p-value in a t-test mean?
faq.a2: The probability of a difference at least as large as yours if the population means were equal. Below your significance level (usually .05), the difference is called significant.
faq.a3: The difference in means in standard deviations. Around 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. Report it with every t-test.
faq.a4: Use two-tailed unless you stated before collecting data that only one direction counts. A one-tailed p is half the two-tailed one, which is why reviewers ask for the reason.
faq.q5: What if my data are not normal?
faq.a5: With 30 or more per group the t-test is usually robust. With small, skewed samples use the Mann-Whitney U test (independent) or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired).

copy.name: How to do a chi-square test
copy.title: How to do a chi-square test of independence
copy.lead: A chi-square test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related, for example whether preference differs between two groups. You will build the table, compute the expected counts, add up the test statistic, find the p-value and check that the test is valid.
copy.result: χ², degrees of freedom, the p-value, Cramér's V and the expected counts for your table.
copy.note: Enter counts of people or things, never percentages or means. Each person must appear in only one cell.
copy.s1t: Open the Chi-square calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Choose Independence for a table of two variables, or Goodness of fit for one variable against expected shares.
copy.s2b: Set the rows and columns and type the observed counts. The example has two groups (rows) and two answers (columns): 20 and 15 in the first row, 30 and 35 in the second, 100 people in all.
copy.s3b: If the variables were unrelated, each cell would hold row total × column total ÷ grand total. The first cell: 35 × 50 ÷ 100 = 17.5. The calculator lists all of them.
copy.s4b: For each cell, square the gap between observed and expected and divide by expected, then add the four results: χ² = 1.10. The degrees of freedom are (rows − 1) × (columns − 1) = 1.
copy.s5b: χ²(1) = 1.10 gives p = .295, far above .05, so there is no evidence of a relationship. Cramér's V = .10 shows the association is weak in any case. Significance needs χ² above 3.84 at 1 df.
copy.s6t: Check the expected counts and report
copy.s6b: The test is reliable when no more than 20 % of expected counts are below 5 and none is below 1; for a small 2 × 2 table use Fisher's exact test. Report it as χ²(1, N = 100) = 1.10, p = .295.
copy.diagram1: Observed counts next to the counts expected if the two variables were unrelated.
copy.diagram2: The chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom: 1.10 is well below the 3.84 needed at α = .05.

faq.q1: What does a chi-square test tell you?
faq.a1: Whether the pattern of counts in a table differs from what you would expect if the variables were unrelated (independence) or if the categories followed given shares (goodness of fit).
faq.q2: How do I calculate degrees of freedom for chi-square?
faq.a2: (rows − 1) × (columns − 1) for a test of independence, and categories − 1 for goodness of fit.
faq.a3: A continuity correction for 2 × 2 tables that makes χ² slightly smaller. It is conservative; many statisticians now prefer Fisher's exact test for small tables instead.
faq.a4: An effect size for the strength of the association, from 0 to 1. For a 2 × 2 table about .1 is small, .3 medium and .5 large.
faq.q5: Can I use percentages in a chi-square test?
faq.a5: No. The test needs the actual counts; percentages hide the sample size and give a wrong result.

copy.name: How to find a p-value
copy.blurb: From z, t, χ² or F.
copy.title: How to find a p-value
copy.lead: Every common test ends in a statistic (z, t, chi-square or F) that has to be turned into a p-value. You will choose the distribution and tails, read the p-value, compare it with α, find critical values and avoid the usual misreadings.
copy.result: The p-value or critical value for any z, t, chi-square or F statistic.
copy.note: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a small p-value does not mean a large or important effect. Always report an effect size as well.
copy.s1t: Open the P-value calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Choose p-value from a statistic, or critical value from α if you want the cut-off instead.
copy.s2b: z for large-sample tests of means and proportions, t for t-tests and regression coefficients, chi-square for tables and goodness of fit, F for ANOVA and comparing variances.
copy.s3t: Enter the statistic and degrees of freedom
copy.s3b: z needs no degrees of freedom. t needs one (n − 1 for one sample), chi-square one, and F two: the numerator and the denominator, for example 2 and 27 in a three-group ANOVA with 30 people.
copy.s4b: Two-tailed tests a difference in either direction and is the usual choice. A one-tailed p is half as large and needs a reason stated in advance. Chi-square and F tests are always right-tailed.
copy.s5b: z = 1.96 two-tailed gives p = .05: the two shaded tails hold 2.5 % each. If p is below your α (usually .05), the result is statistically significant; the calculator also marks .1, .01 and .001.
copy.s6b: Switch to critical value from α: at α = .05 two-tailed it is ±1.96 for z and ±2.228 for t with 10 df; for chi-square with 1 df it is 3.84. Your statistic must pass it to be significant.
copy.diagram1: The same z = 1.96 one-tailed and two-tailed: one tail gives p = .025, two give .05.
copy.diagram2: Two-tailed p-value for z = 1.96: the two shaded tails hold 2.5 % each, 5 % together.

faq.a1: The probability of a result at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means your data would be unusual under the null hypothesis.
faq.a2: .05 is a convention, not a rule. Some fields use .01 or .005, and with very large samples tiny, unimportant differences become significant.
faq.q3: How do I get a p-value from a t-score?
faq.a3: Choose t, enter the t value and its degrees of freedom, and pick one or two tails. The calculator gives the area of the t curve beyond your value.
faq.q4: What is the difference between a p-value and a critical value?
faq.a4: The p-value comes from your data; the critical value comes from α. p < α and |statistic| > critical value are the same decision.
faq.q5: How do I report a p-value in APA style?
faq.a5: Give the exact value to two or three decimals without a leading zero (p = .032), and write p < .001 for anything smaller.

copy.name: How to calculate a z-score
copy.title: How to calculate a z-score
copy.lead: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean, which lets you compare values measured on different scales. You will calculate z, turn it into a percentile, use the 68–95–99.7 rule and work back from a percentile to a value.
copy.result: The z-score and percentile of any value, the value at any percentile, and the probability between two values.
copy.note: Percentiles from z assume a roughly normal (bell-shaped) distribution. For skewed data, use the actual ranks instead.
copy.s1t: Open the Z-score calculator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Choose Value → z-score, Percentile → value, or Probability between two values.
copy.s2b: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ: subtract the mean from the value and divide by the standard deviation. An IQ of 130 with mean 100 and SD 15: (130 − 100) ÷ 15 = 2.
copy.s3b: The share of the normal curve below z is the percentile: z = 2 is above 97.72 % of scores, and only 2.28 % are higher. A negative z lies below the mean.
copy.s4b: About 68 % of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95 % within 2 and 99.7 % within 3. A z beyond ±2 is unusual; beyond ±3 it is rare.
copy.s5t: Go from a percentile back to a value
copy.s5b: x = μ + z × σ. The 90th percentile has z = 1.28, so for IQ it is 100 + 1.28 × 15 = 119.2.
copy.s6t: Find the probability between two values
copy.s6b: Enter both values: between 85 and 115 (z = −1 to 1) lies 68.27 % of the distribution. The curve in the calculator shades the area for you.
copy.diagram1: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ for an IQ of 130 with mean 100 and SD 15.
copy.diagram2: The 68–95–99.7 rule: the share of a normal distribution within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.

faq.a1: How many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. z = 0 is exactly average.
faq.a2: It depends on what is measured: a high z is good for test scores, bad for blood pressure. Values beyond ±2 are unusual whichever way they go.
faq.q3: How do I convert a z-score to a percentile?
faq.a3: Find the area of the normal curve below z: z = 1 is about the 84th percentile, z = −1 the 16th, z = 1.645 the 95th.
faq.q4: What is the difference between a z-score and a t-score?
faq.a4: A z-score uses the known population SD. In a t-test the t statistic uses the sample's SD, so it follows the t distribution, which has heavier tails for small samples.
faq.q5: Can a z-score be greater than 3?
faq.a5: Yes. In a normal distribution only about 0.3 % of values lie beyond ±3, so such values are rare and worth checking for errors.

copy.name: How to cite in APA 7
copy.title: How to cite in APA style (7th edition)
copy.lead: APA style is used across psychology, education, business and the social sciences. You will learn how to write authors and dates, format titles, cite journal articles, books and web pages, use DOIs, cite in the text and lay out the reference list.
copy.result: Correct APA 7 references and in-text citations for your paper.
copy.note: Your university or journal may adjust APA. If its guide differs from these rules, follow the guide.
copy.s1t: Open the APA citation generator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Paste the article's DOI or the book's ISBN and press Find, or type the details yourself. Check every field before copying.
copy.s2t: Write the authors and the date
copy.s2b: Surname, initials: LeCun, Y., Bengio, Y., & Hinton, G. List up to 20 authors, with & before the last. The year follows in brackets: (2015). For a web page add the month and day if given; with no date write (n.d.).
copy.s3b: Use sentence case: capitalize only the first word, the first word after a colon and proper nouns. Article titles stay plain; book and web page titles go in italics.
copy.s4b: For a journal article give the journal name and volume in italics, then the issue in brackets and the pages: Nature, 521(7553), 436–444. For a book give the publisher. For a web page give the site name unless it is the author.
copy.s5t: End with the DOI or URL
copy.s5b: Write the DOI as a link: https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14539. Use a URL only when there is no DOI, and no "Retrieved from" or access date unless the page changes over time.
copy.s6t: Cite in the text and build the list
copy.s6b: In the text use (LeCun et al., 2015) for three or more authors, (Smith & Lee, 2020) for two, or LeCun et al. (2015) in a sentence. The reference list is titled References, sorted alphabetically by first author, double-spaced with a hanging indent.
copy.diagram1: The parts of an APA 7 journal article reference.
copy.diagram2: APA in-text citations for one, two and three or more authors.

faq.q1: What is the difference between APA 6 and APA 7?
faq.a1: APA 7 lists up to 20 authors (6 used 7), drops the publisher location for books, writes DOIs as https://doi.org/ links and uses et al. from the first citation for three or more authors.
faq.q2: How do I cite a source with no author in APA?
faq.a2: Move the title to the author position, before the date. In the text use the title (or a short form) in quotation marks for articles and italics for books.
faq.q3: Do I need page numbers in APA in-text citations?
faq.a3: Only for direct quotations: (LeCun et al., 2015, p. 437). For paraphrases they are optional.
faq.q4: How do I cite a website in APA 7?
faq.a4: Author. (Year, Month Day). Title of page [in italics]. Site Name. URL. Leave out the site name when it is the same as the author.
faq.q5: Does APA use title case or sentence case?
faq.a5: Sentence case for article and book titles in the reference list, title case for journal names and for titles mentioned in the text of your paper.

copy.name: How to cite in MLA 9
copy.title: How to cite in MLA style (9th edition)
copy.lead: MLA style is used in literature, languages and the humanities. You will learn the core elements and their order, how to write authors and titles, how containers work, how to add dates and locations, cite in the text and lay out the works cited page.
copy.result: Correct MLA 9 works cited entries and in-text citations.
copy.note: MLA builds every entry from the same core elements. When a source does not fit an example, add the elements it has in the standard order.
copy.s1t: Open the MLA citation generator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Paste a DOI or ISBN and press Find, or type the details of the article, book, chapter or website yourself.
copy.s2b: Author. Title of source. Title of container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, publication date, location. Skip the elements a source does not have, and keep the punctuation shown.
copy.s3b: Last name, first name: LeCun, Yann. For two authors write the second in normal order: LeCun, Yann, and Yoshua Bengio. For three or more use the first author and et al.
copy.s4b: Use title case. Put the titles of articles, chapters and web pages in quotation marks, and the titles of books, journals and websites (the containers) in italics.
copy.s5b: For a journal: vol. 521, no. 7553, 2015, pp. 436-444. End with the DOI written as https://doi.org/…, or with any other URL without https://. Undated web pages end with Accessed and the date you read them.
copy.s6t: Cite in the text and build the works cited
copy.s6b: In the text give the author and page with no comma: (LeCun et al. 437). The works cited page lists every source alphabetically by its first word, double-spaced with a hanging indent.
copy.diagram1: MLA 9's core elements in order, with a journal article filled in.
copy.diagram2: An MLA in-text citation and the works cited entry it points to.

faq.q1: What is a container in MLA?
faq.a1: The larger whole a source is part of: the journal an article is in, the book a chapter is in, or the website a page is on. Containers are written in italics.
faq.q2: How do I cite a source with no author in MLA?
faq.a2: Start the entry with the title. In the text use a short form of the title in quotation marks or italics, matching the works cited entry.
faq.q3: Do I include URLs in MLA 9?
faq.a3: Yes, for online sources, without http:// or https://. Use a DOI instead when the source has one.
faq.q4: How do I cite page numbers in MLA?
faq.a4: In the text put the page after the author with no comma or "p.": (Smith 45). In the works cited use p. for one page and pp. for a range.
faq.q5: What is the difference between MLA 8 and MLA 9?
faq.a5: MLA 9 keeps the core elements of MLA 8 and adds more guidance and examples, for instance on inclusive language and on citing sources such as social media posts.

copy.name: How to reference in Harvard style
copy.title: How to reference in Harvard style
copy.lead: Harvard is an author–date style used widely in UK, Australian and many other universities. You will learn how to write authors and years, format titles, reference journal articles, books and websites, cite in the text and build the reference list, following Cite Them Right.
copy.result: Harvard references and in-text citations that follow Cite Them Right.
copy.note: Harvard is a family of styles and universities vary in punctuation and details. If your course handbook differs from these rules, follow the handbook.
copy.s1t: Open the Harvard referencing generator on cv.cm
copy.s1b: Paste a DOI or ISBN and press Find, or type the details yourself. For web pages add the date you read the page.
copy.s2t: Write the authors and the year
copy.s2b: Surname, initials, with and before the last author: LeCun, Y., Bengio, Y. and Hinton, G. (2015). With four or more authors use the first and et al. With no date write (no date).
copy.s3b: Put article and chapter titles in single quotation marks and the titles of books, journals and websites in italics.
copy.s4b: For a journal article: Nature, 521(7553), pp. 436–444. For a book: edition (if not the first), place of publication and publisher. Each part follows a fixed order and punctuation.
copy.s5b: End journal articles with Available at: and the DOI link. Web pages add the date you read them: Available at: URL (Accessed: 18 November 2026).
copy.s6t: Cite in the text and build the list
copy.s6b: In the text give the surname and year: (LeCun, Bengio and Hinton, 2015), or LeCun, Bengio and Hinton (2015) in a sentence; add the page for quotations. The reference list is sorted by surname, then year.

copy.diagram2: A Harvard in-text citation and the reference list entry it points to.

faq.q1: What is the Harvard referencing style?
faq.a1: An author–date system: the text gives the author's surname and the year, and a reference list at the end gives the full details in alphabetical order.
faq.a2: No. Harvard has many versions; Cite Them Right is the one most UK universities use. Always check your course handbook.
faq.q3: How do I reference a website in Harvard?
faq.a3: Author or organization (Year) Title of page [in italics]. Available at: URL (Accessed: day Month year).
faq.q4: When do I use et al. in Harvard?
faq.a4: In Cite Them Right, for four or more authors, both in the text and in the reference list. Some universities list all authors in the reference list.
faq.q5: What is the difference between a reference list and a bibliography?
faq.a5: A reference list contains only the sources you cited; a bibliography also lists sources you read but did not cite. Check which one your assignment asks for.
